title: “One of the teachers I work with is bad at their job. Does this hurt my credibility, too?” dibility-too
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Answering a reader question about whether a weak colleague damages one's own credibility, Stuart first reframes what "bad at their job" should even mean, distinguishing genuine credibility-eroding behaviors (yelling, favoritism, phone use during class, slow feedback) from mere disagreement over teaching philosophy or style. He then answers the underlying question directly: yes, a colleague's poor credibility with students can spill over onto other teachers simply by proximity, because students form impressions of a school and its faculty as a whole. But he immediately qualifies that finding with data from his own credibility model, in which roughly 75% of a teacher's credibility comes from their own actions, leaving colleague reputation, parent reputation, and school-wide perception as comparatively minor, uncontrollable factors. The piece lands on a practical reassurance: the spillover is real but small, and not something worth losing sleep over.
points: Stuart separates the credibility question from mere stylistic disagreement, arguing a colleague being "stern and traditional" doesn't make them bad at their job in any credibility-relevant sense.

He supplies a concrete, specific list of the behaviors that do erode student-perceived credibility (yelling, favoritism, blame-shifting, phone use, unearned movie days, slow feedback), giving teachers a diagnostic checklist for their own practice.

His credibility pie chart, roughly 75% your own actions versus a combined remainder from parent, peer, and school reputation, quantifies why colleague spillover is real but shouldn't dominate a teacher's worry.
quotes: Their job isn't to align with your perspectives on teaching. Their job is to promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward mastery of a given subject.
Furthermore, when it comes to Credibility, it's all about what the students believe about the teacher, not what you believe.

The teacher has clear favorites and bends policies and procedures to suit those favorite students. In professional conversations, the teacher tends to blame students for any problems that occur in the classroom and tends to avoid taking responsibility.
So, in these cases, is our Credibility with students hampered by merely working in the same building as these folks? In short, yes. I think so.
Notice that, in that chart, 75% of the influence on your Credibility comes from your actions and the things those actions signal to students.

Yes, your Credibility can be negatively influenced when a given student perceives one or more of your colleagues as bad at their jobs. No, this isn't something for you as a teacher to lose a ton of sleep over. You can only control so much.
